courses.title: Biomechanics and Kinesiology
courses.description: Mechanical principles applied to human movement: forces and levers, joint mechanics, muscle mechanics, posture and gait analysis.

topics.title: Forces, Torque and Levers in the Body
topics.summary: Newton's laws in movement, torque, moment arms and lever systems.

material.heading: Forces and torque
material.body: Biomechanics applies mechanics to living bodies. Kinematics describes motion (displacement, velocity, acceleration); kinetics studies the forces causing it. Forces acting on the body include gravity (acting through the centre of gravity), ground reaction force, muscle forces, friction and external loads. Torque (moment) = force × perpendicular distance from the axis (moment arm); it produces rotation at joints. Holding a load further from the body increases the torque on the spine — the basis of safe lifting (keep loads close, bend knees, avoid twisting).
keyPoints: Keep loads close to the body when lifting

material.heading: Lever systems
material.body: Levers have a fulcrum (axis), effort (muscle force) and load (resistance). First-class levers have the fulcrum between effort and load (e.g. head nodding at the atlanto-occipital joint; triceps extending the elbow). Second-class levers have the load between fulcrum and effort, giving mechanical advantage (> 1) — e.g. rising on tiptoe. Third-class levers have the effort between fulcrum and load (e.g. biceps flexing the elbow) — the most common in the body, with mechanical advantage < 1, favouring speed and range of motion over force. Mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm.
keyPoints: Third class: effort in middle (biceps) — most common

questions.explanation: Torque (moment) = F × moment arm.

topics.title: Joint Mechanics and Arthrokinematics
topics.summary: Degrees of freedom, osteokinematics versus arthrokinematics, roll–glide and joint stability.

material.heading: Joint motion
material.body: Osteokinematics describes the movement of bones (flexion, abduction, rotation) in planes; arthrokinematics describes movements between joint surfaces: roll, glide (slide) and spin. The convex–concave rule: when a convex surface moves on a fixed concave surface, roll and glide occur in opposite directions (e.g. humeral head glides inferiorly during shoulder abduction); when a concave surface moves on a fixed convex surface, roll and glide occur in the same direction (e.g. tibia on femur during knee extension in non-weight-bearing). This guides joint mobilisation direction. Joints have degrees of freedom: hinge (1), condyloid and saddle (2), ball-and-socket (3).

material.heading: Stability and positions
material.body: Joint stability depends on bony congruency, ligaments and capsule, muscles and negative intra-articular pressure. The close-packed position is where joint surfaces are maximally congruent and ligaments are taut (e.g. knee full extension, hip extension with internal rotation and abduction) — joints are most stable but most vulnerable to fracture. The loose-packed (resting) position has maximal joint play, used for mobilisation. The capsular pattern of restriction indicates arthritis (e.g. shoulder: lateral rotation > abduction > medial rotation; hip: medial rotation, flexion and abduction most limited).

questions.stem: Roll, glide and spin between joint surfaces describe:
questions.explanation: Arthrokinematics refers to surface motions within the joint.

questions.stem: During shoulder abduction, the convex humeral head glides:
questions.explanation: Convex-on-concave: roll up, glide down.

questions.stem: When a concave surface moves on a fixed convex surface, roll and glide occur:
questions.explanation: Concave-on-convex: same direction.

questions.stem: A ball-and-socket joint has how many degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: Movement occurs in three planes.

questions.stem: The close-packed position of the knee is:
questions.explanation: Maximal congruency and taut ligaments in full extension.

questions.stem: Joint mobilisation techniques are usually applied in the:
questions.explanation: Maximum joint play is available in the resting position.

questions.stem: The capsular pattern of the shoulder shows greatest restriction of:
questions.explanation: Lateral rotation > abduction > medial rotation.

questions.stem: A hinge joint such as the elbow (humero-ulnar) has how many degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: It moves only in flexion–extension.

topics.title: Muscle Mechanics
topics.summary: Length–tension and force–velocity relationships, muscle architecture and types of work.

material.heading: Force production
material.body: The length–tension relationship: a muscle produces maximal active force at its resting (optimal) length, where actin–myosin overlap is optimal; force falls when it is too short (active insufficiency — e.g. finger flexors cannot grip strongly when the wrist is fully flexed) or too long. Passive insufficiency occurs when a two-joint muscle cannot stretch enough to allow full range at both joints (e.g. tight hamstrings limit hip flexion with the knee extended). The force–velocity relationship: in concentric contraction, force decreases as velocity increases; eccentric contractions generate greater force than concentric ones.
keyPoints: Active insufficiency: two-joint muscle too short
Passive insufficiency: antagonist too short to stretch

material.heading: Architecture and fibre types
material.body: Muscle architecture affects function: parallel (fusiform) muscles have long fibres favouring range and speed (e.g. biceps, sartorius); pennate muscles (unipennate, bipennate, multipennate — e.g. deltoid, rectus femoris, gastrocnemius) pack more fibres, increasing physiological cross-sectional area and force. Fibre types: type I (slow-twitch, oxidative, fatigue-resistant — postural muscles like soleus), type IIa (fast oxidative–glycolytic), type IIx/IIb (fast glycolytic, powerful, fatigable). Strength training increases cross-sectional area (hypertrophy) and neural recruitment; endurance training increases mitochondria and capillaries.

questions.stem: A muscle generates the greatest active force at its:
questions.explanation: Optimal actin–myosin overlap maximises cross-bridges.

topics.title: Posture and Balance
topics.summary: Centre of gravity, base of support, line of gravity, postural deviations and balance systems.

material.heading: Stability and posture
material.body: Stability increases with a wider base of support, a lower centre of gravity (in adults roughly anterior to the second sacral vertebra), and a line of gravity falling within the base of support. In ideal standing posture (lateral view) the line of gravity passes through the ear lobe, the shoulder (acromion), slightly posterior to the hip joint, slightly anterior to the knee joint and anterior to the lateral malleolus. Common postural deviations: excessive thoracic kyphosis, lumbar hyperlordosis, flat back, sway back, forward head posture, and scoliosis (lateral curvature with rotation — assessed with Adam's forward bend test and Cobb angle).
keyPoints: Wider base + lower COG = more stable
Line of gravity: ear, acromion, behind hip, in front of knee

material.heading: Balance
material.body: Balance relies on sensory input from vision, the vestibular system and somatosensory/proprioceptive receptors, integrated by the CNS (cerebellum, brainstem), and motor responses. Postural strategies: ankle strategy (small perturbations on firm surfaces), hip strategy (larger or faster perturbations, narrow surfaces) and stepping strategy (when the centre of mass moves outside the base). The Romberg test (standing with eyes closed) assesses proprioception — loss of balance with eyes closed suggests proprioceptive (dorsal column) loss. Falls in older adults are prevented with balance and strength training (e.g. Otago programme), home hazard modification and medication review.
keyPoints: Falls prevention: balance and strength training

topics.title: Gait Analysis
topics.summary: Phases of the gait cycle, normal gait parameters and common pathological gaits.

material.heading: The gait cycle
material.body: The gait cycle runs from initial contact of one foot to the next initial contact of the same foot (one stride = two steps). Stance phase is about 60% and swing phase about 40% of the cycle at normal speed; double-limb support occurs twice (about 10% each). Rancho Los Amigos terms: stance — initial contact, loading response, mid-stance, terminal stance, pre-swing; swing — initial swing, mid-swing, terminal swing. Normal adult cadence is about 100–120 steps/min and comfortable walking speed about 1.2–1.4 m/s. Running has no double-support phase and includes a flight phase.

material.heading: Pathological gaits
material.body: Trendelenburg gait: the pelvis drops on the swing side due to weak hip abductors (gluteus medius) on the stance side; compensated by lurching the trunk over the stance leg. Antalgic gait: shortened stance on a painful limb. High-stepping (steppage) gait: foot drop from common fibular nerve palsy or L5 radiculopathy. Hemiplegic (circumduction) gait after stroke: the affected leg swings outward with the arm flexed. Parkinsonian gait: shuffling, small steps, reduced arm swing, festination and freezing. Ataxic gait: broad-based and unsteady (cerebellar). Scissoring gait: in spastic diplegic cerebral palsy with hip adductor spasticity. Waddling gait: bilateral hip abductor weakness (e.g. muscular dystrophy, pregnancy).
keyPoints: Antalgic: short stance on painful side

questions.stem: At normal walking speed, the stance phase makes up about ___ of the gait cycle.
questions.explanation: Stance ~60%, swing ~40%.

questions.stem: A stride consists of:
questions.explanation: A stride is from initial contact of one foot to its next contact.

questions.stem: A phase present in walking but absent in running is:
questions.explanation: Running has a flight phase instead.

questions.stem: Pelvic drop on the swing side during walking indicates weakness of the stance-side:
questions.explanation: Trendelenburg gait.

questions.stem: A high-stepping gait to clear the toes suggests:
questions.explanation: Weak dorsiflexors cause the toes to drag.

questions.stem: Shuffling small steps with reduced arm swing and festination are typical of:
questions.explanation: Bradykinesia and rigidity alter gait.

questions.stem: A scissoring gait is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Hip adductor spasticity crosses the legs.

questions.stem: A gait with a shortened stance phase on a painful leg is:
questions.explanation: Patients limit weight bearing on the painful side.
